cues.text: So how did you get on with your school-based research, Phoebe?
cues.speaker: Tony

cues.text: Well, it was exhausting but really valuable.
cues.speaker: Phoebe

cues.text: Good. What was the specific focus you chose?
cues.speaker: Tony

cues.text: My title is ‘Attitudes towards study among eleven-twelve year-old pupils’.
cues.speaker: Phoebe

cues.text: Right. And what made you choose that focus?
cues.speaker: Tony

cues.text: Well, that’s a bit difficult ... lots of my classmates decided on their focus really early on.. .mainly on the basis of what they thought would help in their future career, you know, in their first year’s teaching.
cues.speaker: Phoebe

cues.text: So that’s what helped you decide?
cues.speaker: Tony

cues.text: Actually, it was that I came across a book written by experienced teachers on student attitudes and that motivated me to go for the topic.
cues.speaker: Phoebe

cues.text: Okay. So what were your research questions or issues?
cues.speaker: Tony

cues.text: Well I wanted to look at the ways students responded to different teachers particularly focusing on whether very strict teachers made teenagers less motivated.
cues.speaker: Phoebe

cues.text: And, from your research, did you find that was true?
cues.speaker: Tony

cues.text: No, not from what I saw you know, from my five days’ observation, talking to people and so forth.
cues.speaker: Phoebe

cues.text: OK ... We’ll talk about the actual research methods in a moment, but before that, can you briefly summarise what your most striking findings are.
cues.speaker: Tony

cues.text: Well, what really amazed me was the significant gender differences, I didn’t set out to focus on that but I found that boys were much more positive about being at school ... girls were more impatient, they talked a lot about wanting to grow up and leave school.
cues.speaker: Phoebe

cues.text: Very interesting.
cues.speaker: Tony

cues.text: Yeah ... it is. From doing the research it was clear to me that you might start out to focus on one thing but you pick up lots of unexpected insights.
cues.speaker: Phoebe

cues.text: Right. Did you get any insights into teaching?
cues.speaker: Tony

cues.text: Yes, certainly. I was doing a lot of observations of the way kids with very different abilities collaborate on certain tasks, you know, help each other and I began to realise that the lessons were developing in really unexpected ways.
cues.speaker: Phoebe

cues.text: So what conclusion do you draw from that?
cues.speaker: Tony

cues.text: Well, I know it’s necessary for teachers to prepare lessons carefully but it’s great if they also allow lessons to go their own ways.
cues.speaker: Phoebe

cues.text: Good point. Now, I’m really pleased to see you doing this - analysing and drawing conclusions based on data.
cues.speaker: Tony

cues.text: But surely this isn’t proper data ...
cues.speaker: Phoebe

cues.text: Because it’s derived from such small-scale research? Well, as long as you don’t make grand claims for your findings, this data is entirely valid.
cues.speaker: Tony

cues.text: Hmm .
cues.speaker: Phoebe

cues.text: I like the way you’re already stepping back from the experience and thinking about what you’ve learned about research ... well done.
cues.speaker: Tony

cues.text: But I know I could have done it better.
cues.speaker: Phoebe

cues.text: As you become more experienced you’ll find ways to reduce the risk of difficulties.
cues.speaker: Tony

cues.text: OK.
cues.speaker: Phoebe

cues.text: So, let’s look in more detail at how you gathered your data. Let’s start with lesson observation.
cues.speaker: Tony

cues.text: Well, it generally went quite smoothly. I chose my focus and designed my checklist. Then teachers allowed me into their classes without any problems, which surprised me. It was afterwards that the gruelling work started!
cues.speaker: Phoebe

cues.text: Yeah, it’s very time consuming, isn’t it? Making sense of...analysing ... your observation notes.
cues.speaker: Tony

cues.text: Absolutely. Much more so than interview data, for example ... that was relatively easy to process, though I wanted to make sure I used a high-quality recorder ... to make transcription easier and I had to wait until one became available.
cues.speaker: Phoebe

cues.text: Right. And did you interview some kids as well?
cues.speaker: Tony

cues.text: In the end, yes, I talked to ten, and they were great. I’d imagined I’d be bored listening to them, but.. .
cues.speaker: Phoebe

cues.text: So it was easy to concentrate?
cues.speaker: Tony

cues.text: Sure. One of the teachers was a bit worried about the ethics, you know, whether it was right to interview young pupils, and it took a while for him to agree to let me talk to three of the kids in his class but he relented in the end.
cues.speaker: Phoebe

cues.text: Good. What other methods did you use?
cues.speaker: Tony

cues.text: I experimented with questionnaires, but I really regret that now. I decided to share the work with another student but we had such different agendas it ended up taking twice as long.
cues.speaker: Phoebe

cues.text: That’s a shame ... it might be worth you reflecting on ways you might improve on that for future projects.
cues.speaker: Tony

cues.text: You’re right, yeah.
cues.speaker: Phoebe

cues.text: OK.
cues.speaker: Tony

cues.text: And the other thing I did was stills photography. I didn’t take as many pictures as I’d hoped to.
cues.speaker: Phoebe

cues.text: Lack of time?
cues.speaker: Tony

cues.text: It’s pretty easy just snapping away ... but I wanted each snap to have a purpose, you know, that would contribute to my research aims and I found that difficult.
cues.speaker: Phoebe

cues.text: Well, that’s understandable, but remember...
cues.speaker: Tony
